question: Which approach to the brachial plexus is MOST appropriate for anaesthesia of the forearm and hand while avoiding phrenic nerve block?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The interscalene block reliably blocks the shoulder (C5–C6) but almost universally causes ipsilateral phrenic nerve block — contraindicated in contralateral lung pathology.
The supraclavicular block provides excellent coverage for the entire arm including the hand, but phrenic nerve block occurs in 50–60% of cases due to proximity to C3–C5.

The infraclavicular block targets the cords at the level of the coracoid process and has much lower rates of phrenic nerve block, but axillary provides more distal coverage with near-zero phrenic risk.

Correct. The axillary block targets terminal branches at the axilla, providing reliable forearm and hand anaesthesia with virtually zero risk of phrenic nerve block — the safest choice in patients with contralateral pulmonary compromise.

overallFeedback.feedback: The axillary approach targets terminal nerves below the origin of the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), making it the approach with lowest risk of ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paresis.

Well done. Remember: proximal approaches (interscalene, supraclavicular) = better shoulder coverage but phrenic risk; distal approaches (axillary) = safer for pulmonary patients, limited shoulder coverage.
